name: Computer Science
summary: Learn how computers and software work, from programming and algorithms to operating systems, networks and AI.
overview:
Computer Science is the study of computation: how to describe problems precisely, design efficient solutions, and build reliable software and systems that carry them out. It is more mathematical than many students expect, with discrete maths, logic and algorithms at its core.

The first two years build foundations in programming, mathematics and data structures. The later years cover how real systems work (operating systems, networks, databases), how to build software in teams, and specialist areas like artificial intelligence and security, ending with an independent final-year project.

Graduates work across almost every industry, and the skills transfer well internationally.
durationNotes: 4 years in Nigeria and the US; usually 3 years in England (4 in Scotland), or 4 with a placement year.

subjects: Two of: Chemistry, Biology, Further Mathematics, Economics, Agricultural Science
entryRequirements.notes: Five credits in not more than two sittings. Exact subject combinations vary by university, so check your chosen school's brochure.

subjects: One of: Chemistry, Biology, Economics, Agricultural Science
Further Mathematics, Computer Science or Physics (often preferred)

careers.title: Software engineer
careers.description: Designs, builds and maintains applications and services, usually as part of a product team.

careers.title: Data scientist or ML engineer
careers.description: Builds models that find patterns in data and puts them into production.

careers.title: Cybersecurity analyst
careers.description: Protects systems and networks, investigates incidents and tests defences.

careers.title: Systems or cloud engineer
careers.description: Runs the infrastructure that software depends on: servers, networks and cloud platforms.

careers.title: Product manager
careers.description: Decides what a software team should build next, working between users, engineers and the business.

careers.title: Researcher or lecturer
careers.description: Advances the field through postgraduate research in academia or industry labs.

stages.title: Year 1
stages.summary: Programming foundations and the maths that computer science is built on.

stages.title: Year 2
stages.summary: Core data structures, object-oriented design and how computers work underneath.

stages.title: Year 3
stages.summary: Algorithms, operating systems, networks and building software in teams, plus industrial training.

stages.title: Final year
stages.summary: Specialise in AI, security or systems, and deliver an independent project.

nodes.title: Introduction to Computing
nodes.description: A broad first look at what computers are, how they represent information, and the main areas of computer science you'll meet later in the degree.

nodes.title: Programming Fundamentals
nodes.description: Write your first real programs, usually in Python or C. You'll learn to break problems into steps, use variables, conditions, loops and functions, and debug your own code.

resources.title: MIT 6.0001: Introduction to Computer Science and Programming in Python

nodes.title: Calculus
nodes.description: Limits, derivatives and integrals. Calculus underpins machine learning, graphics, simulation and the analysis of how algorithms grow.

nodes.title: Discrete Mathematics
nodes.description: The mathematics of computer science: logic, proofs, sets, counting and graphs. It teaches you to reason precisely about programs and is the foundation for algorithms and theory.

nodes.title: Command line and Git
nodes.description: The everyday tools of programmers that courses rarely teach: the terminal, a good editor, and version control with Git and GitHub.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education (MIT)

nodes.title: Object-Oriented Programming
nodes.description: Organise larger programs with classes and objects, usually in Java or C++. Covers encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and interfaces.

nodes.title: Data Structures
nodes.description: How to store and organise data so programs stay fast: arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps and graphs, and the trade-offs between them.

nodes.title: Linear Algebra
nodes.description: Vectors, matrices and linear transformations. Essential for graphics, machine learning, data science and scientific computing.

nodes.title: Probability and Statistics
nodes.description: Reason about uncertainty and data: probability rules, random variables, distributions and statistical inference. Key for AI, networking and randomised algorithms.

nodes.title: Digital Logic and Computer Architecture
nodes.description: How a computer works from logic gates up: circuits, the CPU, memory, instruction sets and assembly language.

resources.title: Nand2Tetris: build a computer from first principles

nodes.title: Database Systems
nodes.description: Design and query relational databases: data modelling, SQL, normalisation, indexes and transactions.

nodes.title: Web Development
nodes.description: Build websites and web apps with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and learn how browsers talk to servers. A practical way to build a portfolio early.

nodes.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
nodes.description: Techniques for designing efficient algorithms and proving they are correct and fast: sorting, searching, graph algorithms, divide and conquer, greedy methods and dynamic programming.

nodes.title: Operating Systems
nodes.description: How an operating system shares one machine between many programs: processes, threads, scheduling, memory management, file systems and concurrency.

resources.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (free book)

nodes.title: Computer Networks
nodes.description: How data moves across the internet, layer by layer: from physical links and routing to TCP/IP, DNS and HTTP.

resources.title: Computer Networking video lectures (Kurose and Ross)

nodes.title: Software Engineering
nodes.description: How professional teams build software that lasts: requirements, design, testing, version control, code review and agile processes.

nodes.title: Theory of Computation
nodes.description: What can be computed at all, and how efficiently: finite automata, regular languages, context-free grammars, Turing machines and complexity classes like P and NP.

nodes.title: Human-Computer Interaction
nodes.description: Design software people can actually use: user research, prototyping, usability testing and accessible design.

nodes.title: Industrial training (SIWES or placement)
nodes.description: Work in a real software or IT team. In Nigeria this is the compulsory SIWES placement, usually 6 months; in the UK it's an optional placement year. Keep a logbook: you'll write a report on it.
keyConcepts: Turning it into a job offer

nodes.title: Artificial Intelligence
nodes.description: Classic AI techniques for making computers act intelligently: search, constraint satisfaction, logic, planning, probabilistic reasoning and an introduction to learning.

resources.title: CS50's Introduction to AI with Python (Harvard)

nodes.title: Machine Learning
nodes.description: Build systems that learn from data: regression, classification, neural networks, evaluation, and the maths that makes them work.

nodes.title: Compiler Construction
nodes.description: How source code becomes a running program: lexing, parsing, semantic analysis, interpretation and code generation.

nodes.title: Computer Security
nodes.description: How systems are attacked and defended: cryptography basics, authentication, web and network security, and secure coding.

nodes.title: Distributed and Cloud Computing
nodes.description: Build systems that run across many machines: replication, consistency, fault tolerance, and how cloud platforms deliver them at scale.

nodes.title: Professional Practice and Ethics
nodes.description: The responsibilities that come with building software: privacy, data protection, intellectual property, accessibility and professional codes of conduct.

resources.title: ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct

nodes.title: Final Year Project
nodes.description: Plan, build and write up a substantial piece of independent work under a supervisor, usually a software system or a small research study. It's often the most-discussed item in graduate interviews.

nodes.title: Portfolio and technical interviews
nodes.description: Turn your projects into a portfolio, and practise the data-structure and algorithm problems that most software interviews use.
